title: Vow and Orchard
premise: Jonah Pemberton has spent ten years answering anonymous letters left in the hollow of an old orchard fence, never knowing they came from Marisol Vega, the girl who vanished after a family scandal that cost his father his reputation. When Marisol inherits her grandmother's cottage beside Jonah's coastal research station, she arrives intending to sell quickly and leave before the last ferry of the season. Instead she finds her own handwriting preserved in Jonah's notebooks, and the two must untangle a decade of misdirected letters, a contested inheritance her uncle is stealing through forged documents, and the small found family of station volunteers who refuse to let either of them disappear again. Jonah finally chooses to be seen: he asks her to stay past the last ferry, and together they win back the orchard, turning it into a community sanctuary where their letters began.
about_author: Wendell Yarrow is the pen name of a former tide-pool docent who wrote love letters to strangers for years before writing about them. Vow and Orchard is a second novel rooted in coastal towns where ferries, not clocks, mark the seasons.

chapters.title: The Hollow in the Fence
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He counts nesting turtles at dawn and rereads one of ten years of unsigned letters found in the orchard fence hollow, admitting he's built a life around a stranger's words. Emotional beat: tender loneliness disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Sold Sign, Salt Wind
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She inherits her grandmother's cottage and plans a fast sale, but the ferry schedule, a nosy neighbor's casserole, and the sight of the orchard stall her. Beat: grief arriving late and sideways.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Doesn't Wave
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. First awkward meetings; Jonah is brusque, Marisol defensive. A storm knocks out her power and Jonah's volunteer crew shows up with generators and soup. Beat: found family begins assembling without permission.

chapters.title: Turtle Census
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Marisol volunteers at the station to fill empty days; Jonah teaches her to tag nests, startled by how easily she fits. Beat: reluctant warmth, denial of attraction.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Cleaning the attic, she finds drafts matching the letters Jonah quotes from memory when she glimpses his notebook. She realizes she wrote to him for a decade. Beat: vertigo, guilt, longing.

chapters.title: What My Father Lost
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Flashback to the scandal: Marisol's uncle's forged documents ruined Jonah's father's nursery business, and the family blamed the Vegas wholesale. Beat: old anger complicating new tenderness.

chapters.title: The Ferry Timetable
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She books her departure for the last ferry of the season, telling herself the sale is the point. Jonah overhears. Beat: self-sabotage dressed as practicality.

chapters.title: Night Survey
chapters.summary: Both POV, alternating scenes. A night beach survey goes wrong in fog; stranded until dawn, they talk honestly for the first time—almost. Beat: intimacy under pressure, truth withheld by inches.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Paperwork
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Her uncle Theo arrives 'to help,' pressuring her to sign over the orchard deed. She notices signatures that don't match her grandmother's hand. Beat: suspicion kindling into resolve.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He confronts Marisol with the letters; she confesses she wrote them but stopped after the scandal, believing she'd destroyed his family. Beat: rupture—the revelation cuts both ways.

chapters.title: Silence Between Tides
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Weeks of cold politeness; the volunteer crew plays reluctant matchmakers and accidental mediators. Beat: ache of proximity without contact.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. In the cottage she finds her grandmother's ledger proving Theo embezzled from the orchard stand for years—and that her grandmother knew Jonah's letters were Marisol's all along. Beat: inheritance redefined as obligation and gift.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Offer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The station's elderly archivist, Priya, offers to help authenticate the ledger, revealing she once received letters in the same hollow—from Marisol's grandmother. Beat: the found family deepens across generations.

chapters.title: Forged and Filed
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. With Priya and a retired county clerk, they trace the forged deed through records Theo buried. Justice outside the law takes shape: exposure, not lawsuits. Beat: rising determination, first taste of agency.

chapters.title: Theo Turns the Screws
chapters.summary: Theo's pressure escalates—he threatens to reveal the scandal's ugliest detail involving Jonah's father unless Marisol signs. Beat: fear, moral stakes sharpening.

chapters.title: Confession at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah tells Marisol the full truth his father hid: he took hush money to protect the family, and part of Jonah's silence was shame. Beat: mutual absolution begins; walls cracking open.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. At the harvest meeting, Marisol publicly presents the ledger; neighbors who owed her grandmother testify. Theo's forgery unravels before the community. Beat: cathartic public vindication.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Ash
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Theo leaves in disgrace, but vindication feels hollow; Marisol, unmoored, prepares to leave anyway, convinced she's only brought storms. Beat: darkest hour, love mistaken for damage.

chapters.title: Last Train, Last Ferry
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. On departure day, Jonah races the timetable, reads her own letter aloud at the platform, and asks her to stay after the last train leaves, before the last ferry departs. Beat: climax—vulnerability as courage.

chapters.title: Staying Is a Verb
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She misses the ferry on purpose, terrified and certain, and moves her boxes back inside the cottage. First real kiss in the orchard at dusk. Beat: surrender to being seen.

chapters.title: Deeds and Roots
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Spring: the orchard becomes a community sanctuary co-run by Marisol and the station; the first letter box is replaced with an open mailbox. Beat: justice settled, inheritance honored.

chapters.title: Vow and Orchard
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Under blossoming trees, surrounded by their found family, Jonah and Marisol exchange vows written like letters—signed this time. Final image: turtles hatching at dawn, both watching. Beat: full-circle peace.
